description: Ordered lists, labeled boxes, and the three methods that transform data.

screens.body:
An array is an ordered list of values in square brackets. Each item has a position number called an index — and indexes start at 0, not 1.

So in ["red", "blue", "green"], "red" is at index 0 and "green" is at index 2. The last index is always length - 1.
screens.heading: Arrays: ordered lists
screens.keyPoint: Indexes start at 0. Last index = length - 1.

screens.body:
Arrays grow and shrink. push adds an item to the end; pop removes the last item (and hands it back to you).

These two cover most of what you'll do with arrays day to day — adding new entries and taking the latest one off.

check.question: const letters = ["a", "b"]; letters.push("c"); — what is letters.length now?

screens.heading: Growing and shrinking arrays
screens.keyPoint: push adds to the end. pop takes from the end.

screens.body:
An object is a collection of labeled boxes — each value has a name (a key). It's perfect for describing one thing with several details.

A user has a name AND an age AND an email. An array would lose track of which is which; an object keeps every value labeled.

options: An object — each value gets a labeled key
check.question: To store one user's name, age, and email together, which fits best?

screens.heading: Objects: labeled boxes
screens.keyPoint: Objects bundle related values under named keys.

screens.body:
Dot notation (user.name) is the everyday way to read a value. Bracket notation (user["name"]) does the same thing — and it's required when the key has spaces or lives in a variable.

To add or change a value, just assign: user.age = 20 updates it, user.city = "Calgary" adds a new key.

check.question: The key has a space in it. How do you read it?

code.snippet:
const user = { name: "Roli" };
user.age = 20;              // add a new key
user["favorite color"] = "purple"; // brackets needed for spaces
console.log(user.age);      // 20

screens.heading: Dot vs bracket notation
screens.keyPoint: Dots for normal keys; brackets when keys are tricky.

screens.body:
map transforms every item in an array and returns a NEW array. You hand it a small function that says what to do with one item.

The original array is untouched — map builds a fresh one. That's why it's a favorite: no accidental side effects.
screens.heading: map: transform every item
screens.keyPoint: map builds a new array — one transformed item at a time.

screens.body:
filter keeps only the items that pass your test and returns them as a new array. Your test is a small function returning true (keep it) or false (drop it).

Think of it as a bouncer with a guest list: only items matching your rule get through.
screens.heading: filter: keep what matches
screens.keyPoint: filter returns a new array of only the items that pass.

screens.body:
reduce boils an array down to a single value: a total, a combined string, anything. It walks through the items carrying an accumulator that builds up the answer.

The 0 at the end is the accumulator's starting value. Each step: new total = old total + current item.

check.question: What does [10, 20, 30].reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0) return?

screens.heading: reduce: boil it down to one value
screens.keyPoint: reduce carries a running answer through the array.
